beats.lead: Apple's pinch-to-zoom did not start at Apple.
beats.text: It started with a graduate student who hurt his wrists typing his own dissertation.
beats.note: Wayne Westerman was finishing a PhD on multi-touch surfaces at the University of Delaware when repetitive strain problems pushed him toward low-impact ways of typing.

beats.name: Wayne Westerman and John Elias
beats.role: founded FingerWorks at the University of Delaware to build multi-touch keyboards and pads aimed at people with RSI.

beats.lead: Westerman later explained the real motivation.
beats.text: He wanted computers to feel as expressive as playing the piano.
beats.note: His own words: he had an ergonomic problem and paired it with a motivation, wanting to pull some of a piano's grace into the computer experience.

beats.text: Apple bought FingerWorks in early 2005, taking the patents, the products and both founders.
beats.note: FingerWorks stopped shipping and closed that June. Outside customers only learned a big company had bought them; nobody said which one, or why, for two more years.

beats.text: The iPhone did not arrive until 2007. Its touchscreen came from a keyboard built for sore wrists.

beats.line: Built for pain relief, shipped as magic.
